summary: Defines the syntax of private-key information, including the key and its attributes, and a content type for it. The Cryptographic Message Syntax can sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt it. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 5208.

eli5.summary: A standard box for storing a secret key with notes, that can be locked or signed.

questions: what is an asymmetric key package
subtitle: A standard container for private keys and their attributes, which CMS can then sign or encrypt.

tldr.problem: Systems that move private keys between parties need one agreed syntax for the key, the algorithm it belongs to and any extra information about it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5958 defines the OneAsymmetricKey structure (renamed from PrivateKeyInfo), an Asymmetric Key Package content type that holds one or more of them, and an EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo wrapper. The Cryptographic Message Syntax can then sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt the package.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5208 (PKCS #8 v1.2), adds an optional public key and a version number, and registers the application/pkcs8 media type with the .p8 file extension.

today: RFC 5958 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5208. The unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and What Changed
sections.content:
RFC 5958 defines the syntax for private-key information and a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) content type for it. Private-key information is a private key for a specified public-key algorithm plus a set of attributes. The CMS, defined in RFC 5652, can digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt the content type.

The document obsoletes PKCS #8 v1.2 (RFC 5208). The summary of updates lists the main changes: PrivateKeyInfo was renamed OneAsymmetricKey, a publicKey field and a new version number were added, the Asymmetric Key Package content type was defined, the redundant IMPLICIT on attributes was removed, and requirements for the encoding rule set were added. It also registers the application/pkcs8 media type and the .p8 file extension.

The structures are written in ASN.1, and the key words MUST, SHOULD and so on carry their RFC 2119 meanings.
sections.eli5: This note updates an older standard for storing secret keys. The new version has room for a matching public key and a version label.

sections.title: The Asymmetric Key Package
sections.content:
The asymmetric key package content type transfers one or more plaintext asymmetric keys from one party to another. It is a SEQUENCE SIZE (1..MAX) OF OneAsymmetricKey, so it holds at least one key. Its content type is identified by the object identifier id-ct-KP-aKeyPackage.

Each OneAsymmetricKey has these fields:

  • version: v1 (0) or v2 (1). It is v2 if publicKey is present, otherwise v1.
  • privateKeyAlgorithm: an algorithm identifier, with an object identifier (OID) and optional parameters.
  • privateKey: an OCTET STRING whose format is set by the algorithm. The text gives RSA (RSAPrivateKey) and ECC (ECPrivateKey) as examples.
  • attributes: optional, such as a certificate. Attributes from RFC 2985 MAY be supported.
  • publicKey: optional, a BIT STRING holding the public key.

Generators SHOULD use DER and receivers MUST support BER (which includes DER). In general either the public key or the certificate is present; both together is very rare because it means two copies of the public key.
sections.eli5: Each key goes into its own labelled slot: a version number, what kind of key it is, the secret itself, and optional notes. A package can hold several slots.

sections.title: Encrypted Private Key Info
sections.content:
For use with PKCS #12, the RFC also gives the EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo type. It has two fields: encryptionAlgorithm, which names the algorithm used, and encryptedData, an OCTET STRING holding the encrypted private-key information.

Encryption takes two steps. First the private-key information is encoded to an octet string, where generators SHOULD use DER and receivers MUST support BER. Then that octet string is encrypted with the secret key.
sections.eli5: This is the same key put inside a locked box. The label on the box says which lock was used.

sections.title: Protecting the Package with CMS
sections.content:
The package itself is not protected. The RFC lists CMS content types that can wrap it, from RFC 5652 and RFC 5083.

  • SignedData applies a digital signature.
  • EncryptedData encrypts it when sender and receiver already share the key.
  • EnvelopedData encrypts it when they do not share a key.
  • AuthenticatedData uses message authentication codes.
  • AuthEnvelopedData uses authenticated encryption.

To get the keys back out, the wrapping layers must be removed. The RFC warns that removing the security layers invalidates any signature and may expose the key to unauthorized disclosure.
sections.eli5: The key box can be put inside different kinds of envelopes: one with a seal that proves who sent it, one with a lock, or both.

sections.title: Other Private-Key Formats
sections.content:
Two other formats have been used to move private keys. PKCS #12 (also called P12 or PFX) carries personal identity information. OneAsymmetricKey and PrivateKeyInfo go in its keyBag, and EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo goes in its pkcs8ShroudedKeyBag. The other is Microsoft's proprietary format, whose .pvk extension is used for local storage. The .pvk and .p12/.pfx formats are not interchangeable, though conversion tools exist.

OneAsymmetricKey and PrivateKeyInfo are the same structure, so either can be saved as a .p8 file. A .p8 file is sometimes PEM-encoded: the Base64 of the DER encoding wrapped in the header and footer lines shown below.
sections.eli5: Other tools keep keys in their own boxes. This note says which boxes are the same shape as this one and which are not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Protecting private-key information is vital to public-key cryptography, because disclosing it to another party can lead to masquerades. The encryption algorithm used must be as 'strong' as the key it protects.

The contents of an asymmetric key package are not protected by the content type itself. It can be combined with a security protocol, such as the CMS protecting types, to protect them.
sections.eli5: A secret key must stay secret. The plain box protects nothing, so you need to lock it with something strong.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The CMS content type OID is registered in a DoD arc, and the ASN.1 module OID in an arc delegated by RSADSI to the SMIME Working Group. No further action by IANA is needed for these.

The document registers the media subtype application/pkcs8. It has no required or optional parameters, its encoding is binary, and the file extension is .p8. The PKCS #8 object inside it MUST be a DER-encoded PrivateKeyInfo. The change controller is the IESG.
sections.eli5: The note also gets an official name tag, application/pkcs8, so programs know what a file of this kind contains.

data.title: PEM markers
data.code:
-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
(Base64 of DER-encoded PrivateKeyInfo)
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----

-----BEGIN ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY-----
(Base64 of DER-encoded EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo)
-----END ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY-----
